How FBI Cyber works
FBI Cyber is equipped with a highly skilled and strategically placed workforce, prepared to assist after a cyber incident in the United States and 20 countries. Our mission is rooted in service, driving us to share relevant information and practical tools that can help victims mitigate threats in real time.
With every engagement, we harness our partnerships, expertise, global footprint, and unique investigative and intelligence authorities to support victims:
- The FBI has specially trained cyber squads in each of our 55 field offices, working hand-in-hand with interagency task force partners.
- The FBI leads the National Cyber Investigative Joint Task Force (NCIJTF), a task force of more than 30 co-located agencies from the intelligence community and law enforcement.
- The rapid response Cyber Action Team can deploy across the country within hours to respond to major incidents.
- With cyber assistant law enforcement attachés in embassies across the globe, the FBI works closely with our international counterparts to seek justice for victims of malicious cyber activity.
- The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) collects reports of internet crime from the public. Using such complaints, the IC3’s Recovery Asset Team has assisted in freezing over a billion dollars for victims of cyber crime.
- CyWatch is the FBI’s 24/7 operations center and watch floor, providing around-the-clock support to track incidents and communicate with field offices across the country.
Respond and report
Contact your local FBI field office
If you need to report an ongoing crime, threat to life, or national security threat, file a report at tips.fbi.gov or by contacting your local field office.
File a report with the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
If you are the victim of a cyber-enabled crime or fraud, file a report with the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) as soon as possible. Crime reports are used for investigative and intelligence purposes. Rapid reporting can also help support the recovery of lost funds.

articles.title: City of Osaka warns of data breach impacting 1 million as Japan reels from dozens of cyber incidents
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Osaka, Japan's third-largest city, told its 2.8 million residents to be wary of suspicious emails purporting to come from the local government.
articles.full_text:
City of Osaka warns of data breach impacting 1 million as Japan reels from dozens of cyber incidents
The city of Osaka notified the public that a data breach involving a third-party technology provider exposed more than 1 million email addresses tied to an online administrative services platform.
According to a statement published by the government of Japan’s third-largest city, hackers accessed the Arara email distribution service used by TKC Corporation, the company contracted to maintain the administrative services platform.
Anyone who received an email from the system run by the city between July 2026 and October 31 had their email address leaked, according to the city. They warned the city’s 2.8 million residents to be wary of suspicious emails purporting to come from the city — urging everyone not to open any URLs or attachments.
The city breach came days after the regional government of the Osaka Prefecture announced its own data breach involving the information of food support program participants.
The attack on Arara has had a cascading effect on dozens of large businesses and governments in Japan. The company said a November 2 cyberattack exposed 77 million email addresses from nearly 400 customers, including TKC, gaming giant Sega and others.
Arara noted that hackers used their email distribution service to send millions of malicious emails pretending to be credit card companies and financial institutions.
‘Let us mobilize’
Japan has been rocked by months of cyberattacks on critical companies and institutions — from Japan Airlines to Sony Network Communications and gaming company Capcom.
Last week, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a cabinet meeting on cybersecurity and announced a package of emergency measures aimed at increasing the use of AI for cyber defense, more robust information gathering, offensive cyberattacks and increased support for data breach victims.
About $62 million in emergency funds were dedicated to the effort and companies were urged to report cyberattacks more quickly to government agencies.
“Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities,” she said. “Let us mobilize the full resources of the government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks.”
Japan's national Computer Security Incident Response Team published a study three weeks ago that said it found evidence attackers are using AI to scan for known vulnerabilities before carrying out attacks in the country.
Mihoko Matsubara, the chief cybersecurity strategist at Japanese telecom giant NTT, told Recorded Future News that recent data showed cyberattacks on Japanese systems began to grow in July and skyrocketed through October.
October saw 58% of all reported incidents this year in Japan, she said. About 380 million pieces of personal data have been stolen so far this year.
A large amount of Japanese personal information is already being traded on the dark web, and some of the data has been used for fraudulent securities transactions, Matsubara said, warning that determined actors with financial resources could compile a comprehensive database of Japanese citizens' socioeconomic activities and personal preferences.
Matsubara, who previously worked for Japan’s Ministry of Defense and other government cybersecurity committees, noted that the recent surge in breaches came after new cybersecurity legislation came into effect that allows the government to take more robust action in the event of a significant cyberattack.
“Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan would respond to which kinds of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity,” she said.
Matsubara added that the recent breaches appear to involve AI-tools like Claude and Artex, which help cybercriminals uncover and exploit bugs. But she argued that not every breach in this wave can be attributed to AI.
The most important aspect of the government initiatives announced last week is the acknowledgement that cybersecurity “cannot be left entirely to individual organizations.”
“Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference when push comes to shove,” she said. “However, the funding needs to be the beginning of a consistent longer-term effort, and cannot be seen as a one-time quick fix to the current wave of attacks.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: NYC to bar surveillance pricing as momentum for bans grows nationwide
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The New York City government will be able to fine companies $1,000 for each verified instance of surveillance pricing.
articles.full_text:
NYC to bar surveillance pricing as momentum for bans grows nationwide
The New York City Council has approved a bill barring retailers and other businesses from using surveillance pricing to harness customers’ personal data as a means of charging different people variable amounts for the same product.
The metropolis is the second city in the country to pass legislation banning surveillance pricing, following Seattle, where a similar ban was signed into law last month.
The New York City Council voted 44-5 on Thursday in favor of the bill and Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated its passage, telling the media “when corporations use your personal data to decide what you pay, you only stand to lose.”
The bill allows the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to fine companies deploying surveillance pricing up to $1,000 for each violation, but carves out “bona fide discounts and rewards that are legitimate and transparent, from buy-one-get-one-free deals and loyalty programs to discounts for veterans and students,” according to a council press release.
The bill is a “big deal for a few reasons,” according to Grace Gedye, a Consumer Reports policy analyst who worked on the effort to push it through.
“Once this bill becomes law and goes into effect, it will mean eight million fewer people will have to guess about whether their search history, what they are hovering over online, and more, is shaping the price they see,” Gedye said via email.
“It also means a lot of businesses may need to change their pricing practices — and if they already have to do it for New York City, they may decide to do it for the rest of the country at the same time.”
Gedye noted that the New York state legislature passed a similar surveillance pricing law in June, but said the bill has been sitting unsigned on Gov. Kathy Hochul’s desk for several months. Advocates worry that even if Hochul signs the state legislation, she could use an unusual New York statute allowing governors to unilaterally amend passed bills to weaken its language.
New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland already have similar bans on the books and many more state legislators nationwide are expected to introduce bills when new sessions begin early next year, said George Slover, senior counsel for competition policy at the Center for Democracy and Technology.
‘Viscerally offensive’
“There is a lot of interest around the country in this issue,” Slover said in an interview. “It's viscerally offensive to consumers to think about the fact that they are being basically sized up for their willingness to pay more and eliminate the advantage that they've had all these years, where … the consumer is essentially anonymous when the price is set.”
With the price of food and other consumer goods increasing and data brokers selling businesses detailed consumer profiles — including about spending habits and demographics — there is widespread suspicion that different consumers are being charged varying amounts based on algorithms.
Grocery stores, ride sharing companies and airlines are thought to be widely using surveillance pricing, but public evidence is limited. Lawmakers and regulators are acting anyway.
In October, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) ordered nine food delivery, airline, ride-sharing and retail companies to answer extensive questions about how they exploit personal data to set higher prices for some consumers and less compensation for select employees.
Companies receiving the orders include major airlines, Uber, DoorDash, Walmart and Target.
FTC officials have said they plan to study the “opaque methodology” used to set prices in an era when powerful new technologies, data brokers and algorithms can be easily tapped into to reveal granular information about specific shoppers.
In 2022, Target paid $5 million to settle a lawsuit brought by several California district attorneys who charged the tech giant showed customers’ standing in the parking lot lower prices than those in store.
Last year, a San Francisco news outlet revealed that by changing a web browser’s location, its reporter found customers in the Midwest and Phoenix were charged less than customers in San Francisco for the same New York City hotel rooms.
Advocates have long charged that the Kroger grocery store chain uses surveillance pricing though the company has steadfastly denied the charges.
However, the nonprofit Consumer Reports has revealed Kroger deploys advanced technology to track shoppers' purchases and behaviors, selling the data to third-party companies for targeted advertising. Kroger also has confirmed that it uses digital price tags to quickly tweak pricing though it has said changes are not made based on personal data.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.full_text:
University of Texas at Arlington warns personal information stolen during cyberattack
The University of Texas at Arlington warned students and employees that personal information was stolen by hackers who breached the school’s systems during a cybersecurity incident last month.
In a statement to Recorded Future News, a spokesperson said an investigation into the attack confirmed the stolen data but declined to say what information was obtained by the threat actors.
“We are working to determine whose information may have been involved and the nature and extent of the information accessed. Once we have identified the individuals affected, we will contact them directly with information about what happened, steps they can take to help protect their information, and how the University will support them,” the spokesperson said.
When the attack was initially announced, the university took down MachForms – an online portal used by students and employees for event registration, service requests and surveys.
The spokesperson said MachForms is still offline and the university “continues to monitor for additional impacts to university systems or operations.”
The University of Texas at Arlington is one of the state’s oldest and largest schools, serving more than 41,000 undergraduate and post-graduate students.
The attack on the university was claimed this week by the Qilin ransomware gang, which has quickly become one of the most prominent cybercriminal groups currently operating.
According to data from the Halcyon Ransomware Research Center, the group accounted for 344 alleged ransomware attacks from July to September 2026, the second highest of any group. It recently claimed to be behind an attack on the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF).
One of the group’s leading affiliates was recently arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany. This week, multiple cybersecurity firms and researchers identified one of the group’s leaders as Russian national Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev.
Universities battered by ransomware gangs
University of Texas at Arlington is among a handful of universities currently dealing with the fallout of ransomware attacks.
Canada’s York University confirmed that hackers stole troves of student information dating back more than a decade in a recent cybersecurity incident.
Last week, Vanderbilt University was attacked and said on Wednesday that it will likely “take multiple weeks to fully restore normal operations across all systems.”
“We are prioritizing crucial business operations across the university, including payroll, payment services, admissions, course registration and public safety,” the university said.
They are still investigating what if any data was stolen.
The attack was claimed by the BYOD ransomware gang — a new group researchers have little information on. The same group took credit for recent attacks on Michigan State University and the University of New Mexico.

articles.title: German parliament passes law giving spy agencies hacking, sabotage powers
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In the biggest overhaul of the country’s spy laws of the postwar era, the Bundestag approved the bill by 308 votes to 190 — with 71 abstentions — months after Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s cabinet signed off on the draft.
articles.full_text:
German parliament passes law giving spy agencies hacking, sabotage powers
German lawmakers passed legislation Friday allowing the country’s intelligence agencies to hack foreign systems, sabotage adversaries’ supply chains and take down servers run by hostile state-backed hackers.
In the biggest overhaul of the country’s spy laws of the postwar era, the Bundestag approved the bill by 308 votes to 190 — with 71 abstentions — months after Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s cabinet signed off on the draft.
At the time the powers were proposed, Chancellery chief Nina Warken said they could allow the nation’s agencies to use cyber operations to sabotage drone factories or chemical weapons laboratories and to disable servers run by hostile state-sponsored hackers.
Intelligence reform is a sensitive subject in Germany, where the shadows cast by both the Gestapo and Stasi remain within living memory. But, as with the country’s increased military spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the government has pointed to a rapidly changing threat environment to justify the legislation.
Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the bill the “reform of the century” during the Bundestag debate, saying the new powers would turn the country’s agencies into “genuine intelligence services” operating “on equal footing with our European partners.”
Rewriting the laws governing both Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, and its domestic agency for the protection of the constitutional order, the BfV, the government bill gives the BND powers to act against threats abroad rather than simply report on them.
The BfV gets a shorter list of covert powers inside Germany, such as blocking or rerouting data traffic, but it remains prohibited from using force against people — something which remains the sole prerogative of law enforcement in the country.
Both agencies also gain a legal basis to analyze large datasets with AI and to match images biometrically against material found online.
Warken, who is responsible for the BND, told lawmakers that foreign powers target Germany covertly every day, disguising “sabotage as an accident, espionage as business dealings, and propaganda as an opinion.”
The new reforms would let the BND act “when no one else can,” she added, for instance by shutting down the servers of a state hacking group stealing data from critical infrastructure companies.
Berlin has grown increasingly vocal about such threats, something which officials have linked to Berlin’s support for Ukraine. Last December, Germany summoned the Russian ambassador over a cyberattack on its air traffic control authority that it attributed to APT28, and over a disinformation campaign aimed at influencing its federal election.
During that campaign, fake videos were circulated which appeared designed to foment discontent among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party, showing the AfD missing from ballot papers, or ballot papers marked in support of the party being shredded.
The confirmed powers stop well short of those exercised by some of Germany’s closest allies. The bill bars the intelligence agencies from measures intended to endanger a person’s life or physical safety, leaving the BND without anything resembling the paramilitary capabilities of France’s DGSE or the CIA’s Special Activities Center.
Amendments
Lawmakers on the interior committee made a series of last-minute amendments to the cabinet’s draft this week, including providing both agencies with the authority to order telecom providers to “freeze” traffic data they expect to need, preserving it until the legal conditions for accessing it are met.
The power is narrower than those available to the agency’s counterparts in Britain, France and the United States. Telecommunications companies can be required to retain communications data for up to a year in Britain and France, while U.S. government agencies can order providers to preserve records for up to 180 days without a court order under the Stored Communications Act.
The BND will be allowed to retain metadata collected during bulk surveillance activities for 13 months rather than 12, and the BfV gains authority to investigate organized crime groups that support extremism, work normally left to the police.
Other changes stipulate safeguards that limit the agencies’ activities — including protecting Germans’ messages and queries sent to chatbots and search engines from BND surveillance in the same way as person-to-person communication.
The amendments also strengthen protections for doctors and other medical professionals, though critics note that journalists and lawyers are left with weaker safeguards.
The agencies’ hacking operations and active measures inside Germany will need advance approval from the Independent Control Council, the agencies’ oversight body, whose court-like panel has been doubled from six to twelve members.
One amendment drew fire from the far right, as it allows the BfV to restrict information-sharing with individual state intelligence offices if there are concrete indications that federal or state security interests are at risk. The move requires the agreement of a majority of state offices, although the BfV can act alone in urgent cases.
AfD lawmaker Christian Wirth called the provision a “Lex AfD,” which he said was designed to cut off states whose governments the coalition dislikes.
The BfV had classified the AfD as a confirmed right-wing extremist group last year, but a court in Cologne put that label on hold while it considers the party’s legal challenge.
Until that challenge is settled, the agency is legally only permitted to monitor the AfD as a suspected extremist group, a categorization that limits both the surveillance it can use and what it can say about the party in public.
Intelligence agencies in several of Germany’s eastern states, including Saxony and Thuringia, have separately labeled their local AfD branches as confirmed extremists.
The party has never led a state government, although its support has increased in recent years.
In September, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, its best result in any state election, though not enough for a majority. Two weeks later, it came first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Saxony-Anhalt’s previous CDU-led government remains in office as a caretaker while other parties refuse to work with the AfD.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.
IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.
Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.
The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.
Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.
Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.
What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”
